B: Hiya! Can you hear me okay?
A: Ar, I can hear you. Is it just three minutes, this?
B: Yeah, I think so, there's like a timer thing. I'm Ellie, by the way.
A: Kelly. Sorry, I'm a bit frazzled, I've just got in off an early and my daughter's been on at me about her blazer the whole way home.
B: Oh no, what's wrong with the blazer?
A: Nothing's wrong with it, that's the point. She just won't wear it. She's eleven, just started big school, and apparently nobody wears their blazer, so she carries it in her bag all screwed up and I get a phone call. Do you know what I mean? I'm like, I paid forty quid for that.
B: Forty quid! That's mad. I remember doing that, though, sorry. My mum used to go spare.
A: See, you're on her side. Where are you then?
B: Barnstaple, so North Devon. Kind of near the coast.
A: Oh, very nice. I'm Walsall. No coast. We've got the canal.
B: Aw, canals are nice though!
A: They're alright. There was a shopping trolley in ours last week, somebody put it on the Facebook group, and it turned into a massive row, sixty comments about whose trolley it was. I was in there an' all, I couldn't help meself.
B: That's so funny. Our local group's the same, it's all people moaning about seagulls.
A: Seagulls. Ha. Go on, what do you do then? Your hoodie's got a logo, I clocked that.
B: Yeah, I'm a lifeguard at the leisure centre, and I teach kids' swimming lessons in the evenings and Saturday mornings. I love the lessons, honestly. There's a little boy in my Saturday class who's been proper scared of the water for weeks, and this Saturday he swam a whole width without armbands, and I nearly cried on poolside. His mum did cry. Sorry, I'm rambling.
A: No, that's nice, that. Bet you're shattered though, with the hours.
B: Proper shattered. I did a six o'clock open and then covered a late, so I'm kind of running on Haribo. What about you?
A: Care assistant. Old people's home, part-time, twenty-odd hours. Earlies mostly, the odd weekend.
B: Oh, that must be hard, like, physically?
A: My back's knackered, yeah, the hoisting. But the residents are the best bit. There's one lady, she's got dementia, and she calls me Doreen every single shift, which is my nan's name. I just go along with it now. I'm Doreen on a Tuesday. It's the paperwork and the managers I can't stand, not the residents.
B: Aw, I love that though. Being Doreen.
A: It's alright. The pay's rubbish for what it is, but you was asking.
B: Is it, like, something you always wanted to do?
A: Erm, not really, it sort of just happened. I did a bit of hairdressing at college, dropped out, kids came along. You fall into stuff, don't you. I keep saying I'll do nails from home.
B: Your nails are nice, I saw them in the photo!
A: One's chipped, don't look. Do you get paid for these quick, do you know? I'm still waiting on a voucher from another one.
B: Oh, I don't actually know, sorry, I didn't even check. I just thought it sounded kind of fun.
A: Fun. Ha. You're young, you'll learn. Are you not at uni or nothing then?
B: No, everyone from school went, and I kind of just stayed. But I'm saving for Australia, like a working holiday, maybe in a couple of years.
A: Good on you. Go. Honest, go while you can, before you've got two kids eating everything in your fridge.
B: That's what my nan says!
A: Your nan's right. I went Tenerife once before the kids and I still think about it. Seriously, I'd go tomorrow if I wasn't skint.
